code:
enum E { A, B, C }
void main(){ IO.print(E.values().length); }
explanation: values() returns an array of all enum constants in declaration order.
teachBack: What does values() return?

code:
enum E { A, B, C }
void main(){ IO.print(E.A.compareTo(E.C)); }
explanation: Enums implement Comparable by declaration order; A (index 0) compared to C (index 2) is negative.
teachBack: How does an enum's compareTo order constants?

options.text: it is final and compares with ==
it compares by ordinal value only
it throws for different enum types

explanation: Enum.equals is made final and simply uses reference identity (==). Enum constants also implicitly extend java.lang.Enum and implement Comparable.
teachBack: Why can enum constants be compared with ==?

code:
record R(int x){ R(String s){ this(Integer.parseInt(s)); } }
void main(){ IO.print(new R("7").x()); }
explanation: A non-canonical constructor has a different signature and must call another constructor of the same record with this(...); here it parses then delegates to the canonical one.
teachBack: What must every non-canonical record constructor do?

code:
record R(int x){ public R(int x) throws Exception { this.x = x; } }
void main(){}
explanation: A canonical constructor may not declare a throws clause (its body may still throw unchecked exceptions).
teachBack: Which clauses are forbidden on a canonical constructor?

code:
record R(int x){ { IO.print("i"); } }
void main(){}
explanation: A record may have static initializers but not instance initializers, so this does not compile.
teachBack: Which kind of initializer can a record have?

code:
record R(int x){ static int n; static { n = 5; } }
void main(){ IO.print(R.n); }
explanation: A record may declare static fields and static initializers (but not instance fields or instance initializers).
teachBack: What is the difference between what a record and a class may declare?

code:
interface I { int X = 5; }
void main(){ IO.print(I.X); }
explanation: Interface fields are implicitly public static final, so I.X is a constant.
teachBack: What modifiers apply to every field declared in an interface?

explanation: Interface fields are inherited and can be accessed through an implementing class name (unlike interface static methods).
teachBack: Why can you access I.X via C, when static interface methods are not inherited?

explanation: When a class inherits a method from its superclass and a default from an interface, the superclass version wins outright.
teachBack: Why does the superclass method take precedence over the interface default?

code: void main(){ IO.print(java.util.function.Function.identity().apply("x")); }
explanation: Function.identity() returns a Function whose apply returns its input unchanged.
teachBack: What does Function.identity() return for any input?

explanation: Flow scoping: with a negated instanceof, the pattern variable s is in scope only in the else branch, where it is known to be a String.
teachBack: Where is the pattern variable in scope when the instanceof is negated?

explanation: Multiple pattern variables can be combined with &&, each bound in the true scope of the condition.
teachBack: How do you test two objects and use both pattern variables?

explanation: A record pattern deconstructs the record, binding a and b to its components.
teachBack: What does a record pattern bind?

explanation: A reference-type selector triggers pattern matching; 5 is an Integer so the Integer pattern matches.
teachBack: What makes a switch a pattern-matching switch?

explanation: Pattern matching also works with the old colon+break syntax; break is required after each label because fall-through is not allowed in pattern switches.
teachBack: Do pattern switches allow fall-through?

explanation: var is not a type, so you cannot write var[] or use it as a type name.
teachBack: Why is `var[] a` illegal?

explanation: var may be used for lambda parameters, but parentheses are required: (var a) -> ...
teachBack: What is required when using var in a lambda parameter list?

explanation: An unnamed variable _ can be used for a catch parameter you do not need to read.
teachBack: Where else can unnamed variables be used besides local declarations?

explanation: A synchronized static method locks the Class object's monitor (one per class), so the two increments are serialized.
teachBack: Which monitor does a synchronized static method use?

explanation: Once a permitted subclass is marked non-sealed, it can be extended freely, and its subclasses remain subtypes of the sealed type.
teachBack: What does marking a subclass non-sealed allow?

explanation: Java 25 flexible constructor bodies let a constructor run statements that initialize its own fields before calling super(). super() then runs P's constructor, and x is read afterward.
teachBack: What may a constructor do before super() in Java 25?

explanation: An overriding method may not widen the checked exceptions; it may narrow them or declare none.
teachBack: How may an overriding method change the throws clause?

explanation: A final method cannot be overridden, so this does not compile. (A static method cannot be overridden either.)
teachBack: Which methods can never be overridden?

explanation: An overriding method may not be less accessible than the overridden one; package-private is less accessible than protected.
teachBack: What accessibility rule applies to overriding methods?

explanation: Static methods are hidden, not overridden. The call is resolved by the reference type (A), so A.who() runs.
teachBack: Why does a.who() call A's version even though the object is a B?

code:
abstract class A {}
void main(){ new A(); }
explanation: An abstract class cannot be instantiated, whether or not it has abstract methods.
teachBack: Can an abstract class with no abstract methods be instantiated?

prompt: Which four kinds of methods may an interface contain?
explanation: Interfaces may declare abstract (public), static (public or private), default (public), and private methods. No protected, final, or native methods.
teachBack: Which access modifiers are allowed on interface methods?

prompt: Is the @FunctionalInterface annotation required for an interface to be functional?

options.text: no; any interface with exactly one abstract method is functional
only for interfaces in the JDK

explanation: @FunctionalInterface is optional; it just asks the compiler to verify the single-abstract-method shape.
teachBack: What does @FunctionalInterface add?

prompt: Which is TRUE about garbage collection?

options.text: circular references prevent an object from being collected
code can only request GC; circular references do not prevent collection
objects in the string pool can never be collected

explanation: Java cannot force GC (System.gc() is only a request), and circular references do not stop collection when nothing reachable refers to the cycle.
teachBack: Why don't circular references leak memory in Java?

explanation: try-with-resources accepts a pre-declared resource variable (try(r)), as long as it is final or effectively final. Body prints t, then close prints c.
teachBack: What two forms may the resource list take?

explanation: A resource must be a variable declaration or a pre-existing variable reference, not an assignment expression.
teachBack: Why is `try(r = new R())` invalid?

explanation: Each resource needs its own declaration statement; you cannot declare two variables in a single declaration inside the resource list.
teachBack: How do you declare two resources of the same type?

explanation: A resource variable's scope is the try block, so it is not visible in finally.
teachBack: What is the scope of a try-with-resources variable?

explanation: A resource variable must be final or effectively final; r is reassigned, so it cannot be used as a resource.
teachBack: Why must a resource variable be effectively final?

explanation: When the body throws nothing but close() does, the first close exception (from b, closed first) is propagated and the next (from a) is added to its suppressed list.
teachBack: In this situation, which exception reaches the caller and what happens to the others?

explanation: Array equals/hashCode are identity-based (inherited from Object), not content-based. Use Arrays.equals to compare contents.
teachBack: How do you compare two arrays by content?

explanation: Arrays are objects of synthetic classes; an int[] is class [I, a boolean[] is [Z, and so on.
teachBack: What is the class name of an int[] and of a boolean[]?

explanation: binarySearch returns the index of the key in a sorted array (1 for element 3).
teachBack: What does binarySearch require of the array?

explanation: mismatch returns the index of the first differing element (1), or -1 if the arrays are equal.
teachBack: What does mismatch return when the arrays are identical?

explanation: compare returns a negative value when the first array is lexicographically smaller (2 < 3 at index 1).
teachBack: What does a negative result from Arrays.compare mean?

explanation: Set.copyOf silently ignores duplicates (unlike Set.of, which throws IllegalArgumentException).
teachBack: How does Set.copyOf handle duplicates compared with Set.of?

explanation: List.of copies its elements and is independent from the source array, unlike Arrays.asList which is a view.
teachBack: How does List.of differ from Arrays.asList regarding the backing array?

explanation: Iterator.remove() throws IllegalStateException if next() has not been called (or remove was already called once).
teachBack: When does Iterator.remove() throw IllegalStateException?

explanation: ArrayDeque supports FIFO: addLast appends and pollFirst removes the head, so the first element added (1) comes out.
teachBack: How do you use an ArrayDeque as a stack vs a queue?

explanation: A Set ignores duplicates, determined by equals/hashCode; adding 1 twice leaves one element.
teachBack: What decides whether a HashSet treats two elements as duplicates?

explanation: ArrayList allows null elements (and duplicates), unlike ArrayDeque or the factory lists.
teachBack: Which collections here reject null elements?

explanation: LinkedHashMap implements SequencedMap, so firstEntry()/lastEntry()/reversed() reflect encounter order.
teachBack: Name three methods SequencedMap adds.

explanation: getOrDefault returns the mapped value or the default when the key is absent.
teachBack: How does getOrDefault differ from get?

explanation: Arrays.asList allows null and duplicate values (it is a fixed-size view over the array).
teachBack: How does Arrays.asList differ from List.of regarding nulls?

prompt: Which Collection method removes all elements that match a predicate?
explanation: removeIf(Predicate) removes matching elements; removeAll(Collection) removes those contained in another collection; retainAll keeps only the intersection.
teachBack: What is the difference between removeAll and retainAll?
